original_value: AbstractWe present an interactive approach to analyse flow fields using a new type of particle system, which is composed of autonomous particles exploring the flow. While particles provide a very intuitive way to visualize flows, it is a challenge to capture the important features with such systems. Particles tend to cluster in regions of low velocity and regions of interest are often sparsely populated. To overcome these disadvantages, we propose an automatic adaption of the particle density with respect to local importance measures. These measures are user defined and the systems sensitivity to them can be adjusted interactively. Together with the particle history, these measures define a probability for particles to multiply or die, respectively. There is no communication between the particles and no neighbourhood information has to be maintained. Thus, the particles can be handled in parallel and support a real‐time investigation of flow fields. To enhance the visualization, the particles' properties and selected field measures are also used to specify the systems rendering parameters, such as colour and size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on different simulated vector fields from technical and medical applications.

result.paraphrase: Abstract We propose an interactive method for analyzing flow fields with a new particle system made up of autonomous particles that explore the flow. Although particles offer an intuitive way to visualize flows, capturing key features with such systems is difficult: particles cluster in low-velocity regions, while regions of interest are often sparsely populated. To address this, we automatically adapt particle density according to local importance measures. These measures are user-defined, and the system’s sensitivity to them can be interactively adjusted. Combined with particle history, they determine the probability that particles multiply or die. Because there is no communication between particles and no neighborhood information needs to be maintained, the particles can be processed in parallel and support real-time flow-field investigation. For improved visualization, particle properties and selected field measures also define rendering parameters such as color and size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach on different simulated vector fields from technical and medical applications.
